svg.text: How as_a_operand works: the same 32 values, new labels
The idea in one sentence: after S = Q·Kᵀ, each thread already holds exactly the values of P that the next multiply, O += P·V,
will ask it for, and even in the same order. Only the labels CuTe uses to find them differ. as_a_operand changes the labels,
so P goes straight from one multiply into the next without moving. The steps below check this for one thread, thread 0.
What thread 0 holds: 32 values of P, numbered 0–31
Warp 0 computes rows 0–15 of P (all 64 keys), and its 32 threads share the 16 × 64 = 1,024 values: 32 each. Which 32 is not
our choice: the tensor-core instruction (mma.m16n8k16) fixes it. It produces S in tiles of 16 rows × 8 keys, and in every tile it
gives thread 0 the same 4 spots: rows 0 and 8, the tile's first 2 columns. Thread 0 numbers its values tile by tile:
Tile n holds values 4n to 4n + 3, in the order (row 0, 1st column), (row 0, 2nd column), (row 8, 1st column), (row 8, 2nd column).
This is the accumulator view: CuTe labels value i by (spot in the tile, tile n).
What O += P·V asks thread 0 for: 4 steps of 8 values
The next multiply reads P 16 keys at a time (4 steps, k = 0 to 3). The same instruction fixes which values of each 16 × 16 piece
thread 0 must hand in, and in what order (slots 0–7): rows 0 and 8, columns 0, 1, 8 and 9 of the piece.
Compare with step 1: the marked cells are the same 32 spots. Every value the multiply wants from thread 0 is one it already holds.
This is the A-operand view: CuTe labels each value by (slot in the step, step k).
Same values, same order: only the grouping differs
Line thread 0's 32 values up in its own order, 0 to 31. Above: the accumulator view groups them in 8 tiles of 4. Below: the
A-operand view groups them in 4 steps of 8. Step k is simply values 8k to 8k + 7, already in slot order 0–7.

svg.text: Check one: value 13 is tile 3 (keys 24–31), row 0, 2nd column, so key 25. In the A view it is step 1, slot 5: row 0, column 9 of keys 16–31,
so key 25 again. The same holds for all 32 values (checked on the GPU).
Why it lines up: one 16 × 16 step is two neighbouring 16 × 8 tiles side by side, and the instruction places thread 0's spots the same way
in both: the first 4 slots of step k are tile 2k, the last 4 are tile 2k + 1.
The code only rewrites the labels
CuTe finds a thread's values through a layout: shape (how many along each direction) : stride (how many values to jump for each step
along it). Each layout here has three parts: the values in one group, the groups down (always 1, stride 0), the groups across.

svg.text: move the tile-in-pair into the group: 8 values per step; 4 steps, 8 apart
make_tensor(acc.iterator, layout) puts the new layout on acc's own values: acc.iterator is where they start. No value is copied or moved,
and no instruction is generated. Read the new layout like step 3: value = slot + 8 × step (the first part counts 0–7, the last jumps by 8).
Using it: step k of P is read straight from thread 0's own values

svg.text: cute.gemm(tiled_mma, acc_O, tOrP[None, None, k], tOrVt[None, None, k], acc_O)
tOrP[None, None, k] means: all 8 slots of step k, which are values 8k to 8k + 7. The multiply reads them where they already are.
Before Round 3, P was written to shared memory and read back just to arrive in this order, which it already had.
